title: Ockham's razor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Duns Scotus and haecceity, thisness. Your line was this one, loved.

The car is making a noise. A friend says it might be the transmission, or a curse, or a raccoon living in the engine. The mechanic opens the hood and finds a loose heat shield. Start with the simplest story that explains the noise; don't add raccoons you don't need. That habit has a name, and it belongs to a friar. William of Ockham was a Franciscan, like Scotus yesterday. His blade is called Ockham's razor.

One of Ockham's own Latin wordings goes like this: plurality is not to be posited without necessity. In plain English, don't multiply things without need. When two explanations cover the facts, keep the one with fewer moving parts. The rule later got a nickname, a razor, because it shaves away whatever does no work. Ockham used it on the philosophy of his day. Some teachers, he thought, had stacked invisible extras on top of the world, layer on layer, and he kept asking a plain question: do we need that? Often his answer was no. Yet the friar's razor didn't shave away God. For Ockham, much of what Christians hold about God isn't proved by clever argument at all. It rests on God's free revelation, received in faith. So the razor cleared clutter out of philosophy and left trust where it was. Jesus asked for plain speech too. Speaking about oaths in the Sermon on the Mount, he says, "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." Say yes, mean yes, and stop. And when Martha was rushing around her house with guests to feed, he told her, "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful." Ockham's razor isn't a rule for faith. It's a rule for honest thinking: explain what you need to explain, and leave the raccoons out. That closes a week that walked from John of Damascus to Anselm, Abelard and Heloise, Aquinas and Scotus.

Bring to mind one story you've been telling yourself, why a friend hasn't texted back, why today feels off, and notice how many parts it has: hidden motives, secret plans, a whole plot. Then pick up the razor and hold the simplest explanation that fits what you actually know; maybe they're busy, maybe you're tired. If you pray, you can hand the leftover worry to God.
Ockham's razor. Don't multiply things without need: keep the simplest explanation that fits, and shave off the rest.
Your line: keep it simple. One thing is needful. That's day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Christian thinkers and teachers use the principle of not multiplying explanations in philosophy and theology, while holding that much of what they believe about God rests on revelation received in faith rather than on proof.

chat.says: Doesn't Ockham's razor just shave God right out of the picture?
options: Not for Ockham. He used it on philosophy's clutter; faith in God rested on revelation.
Yes. Ockham used his razor to show that believing in God is simply unnecessary.
No, because Ockham's razor says the most complex answer is always the truest.
chat.meaning: Ockham's razor shaves away what does no work in an explanation. For Ockham, much of what Christians hold rests on God's revelation, received in faith.
